newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Two Western captives freed by Tajik rebels.
newsitem.headline: Two Western captives freed by Tajik rebels.

text.p: A Briton and a South African captured by guerrillas in war-torn Tajikistan were freed on Saturday, the head of their mining company said.

"They have been released. They are now in (the Tajik capital) Dushanbe and they are in good form," Robert Mendelsohn, head of London-based Gold and Mineral Excavation Ltd, told Reuters in the neighbouring republic of Uzbekistan.

The Briton, Alex Lemon, and the South African, Barrent Knotze, were held by Tajik Islamist fighters for nearly three weeks after the mine where they were working, in Darvaz in the south of the former Soviet republic, came under their control.

Two Tajiks also working for the company and taken captive by the guerrillas were freed along with the two Westerners, Itar-Tass news agency reported. The release of all four men was delayed by bad weather, it said.
Mendelsohn said the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and British diplomats were all involved in securing the Westerners' release.

The company kept the story out of the public eye for fear of jeopardising their employees' chances of release. Mendelsohn refrained from using the word "hostages" and said the two men were just "unexpected guests" of the Tajik rebels.
Lemon, later contacted in Dushanbe by telephone, declined to make any immediate comment on his release or time spent in captivity but sounded cheerful.
In London, the Foreign Office said it was "delighted by the news of the captives' release" and confirmed that Lemon was "in good health and spirits".
It said the British embassy in Tashkent had been in close contact with the rebels and their captives but gave no further details.
Mendelsohn's company, which produced about one tonne of gold at the mine this year, is one of two mining gold in the remote mountainous republic bordering Afghanistan and China.

Tajikistan's secular government and the Islamist opposition signed an accord in Moscow last week aimed at ending a bitter four-year civil war that has killed tens of thousands and has displaced many more.
